rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says rajfah means torment, not necessarily an earthquake; he thinks a destructive northern ṣarṣar storm struck and killed people face down.
rows.anchor: It merely signifies a torment. It seems that the northern wind called ṣarṣar blew in the form of a storm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here dār means diyār; the Qur’an's wording about the Thamūd in Hūd 11:65 and 11:67 clarifies the term.
rows.anchor: Thus in verse 65 of S ūrah Hūd, the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ's final address came after the she-camel was killed but before the punishment, and he left his people after speaking.
rows.anchor: These words constitute the last address of Ṣāliḥ (sws) to his nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This follows God's practice of moving messengers from doomed places; the three-day respite after the camel's killing also gave Ṣāliḥ and his companions time to leave.
rows.anchor: given a further respite of three days.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment is narrated immediately after the camel's killing to stress the crime's consequence; Islahi links this ordering to Shuʿayb's story and Hūd 11:42–45.
rows.anchor: To highlight the immediate consequence of the crime, the torment is mentioned right after the killing of the she-camel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeatedly saying “O my people” expresses a duty to one's nation and country, whose right is comparable to the rights of oneself and family.
rows.anchor: in a similar way, his nation and country also have this right.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sincere, sympathetic, concerned well-wisher fulfills this duty; such a person succeeds before God and is not accountable for the nation's destruction, while neglect brings accountability.
rows.anchor: full sincerity, sympathy and concern.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the statement as fact, not sorrow alone: in a corrupted society, champions of divine wrath become heroes and rescuers enemies, like a patient preferring advice that worsens illness.
rows.anchor: The sentence “but you do not like well-wishers” does not merely express sorrow at their response; it is also a statement of fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was Abraham's nephew, and his people lived south of Syria around the Jordan.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) was Abraham’s (sws) nephew. His people lived in the area that lies to the south of Syria around the river Jordan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike Hūd and Ṣāliḥ, Lot is called a messenger to “his nation” rather than its brother, because he preached to them without belonging to them by lineage.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this that his nation was regarded to be his because he preached to them and not because he belonged to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers are made known to their people through lineage or long residence; Lot had lived among his audience and likely married there, while Moses likewise knew Pharaoh's people through long residence.
rows.anchor: God’s established practice is that a messenger belongs to the nation he preaches.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-fāḥishah means blatant sexual impropriety and lewdness.
rows.anchor: The word ْﻟﻔﺎﺣﺸﺔ in the verse means blatant sexual impropriety and lewdness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative wording is meant to express disgust and aversion.
rows.anchor: The interrogative nature of the sentence is meant to express disgust and aversion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Lot leaves the act unnamed, Islahi infers it was so widespread that everyone recognized it.
rows.anchor: This quite evidently shows that such was its rampant nature in the society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi parses mā sabaqakum bihā as an independent sentence, not an adjective of al-fāḥishah; if adjectival, al-fāḥishah would lack the definite article.
rows.anchor: is not an attribute of ْﻟﻔﺎﺣﺸﺔ Had it been so, the latter should have occurred without the definite article.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot expresses disgust in two ways: he calls the deed a manifest indecency and says no earlier people had done it.
rows.anchor: Here Lot (sws) has expressed his disgust on this wrongdoing in two different ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No nation before you” need not mean no earlier person ever committed the act; ahad can denote a plurality, and the point may be that no society made it a way of life.
rows.anchor: The words “no nation before you has perpetrated it” do not necessarily mean that this indecency was not perpetrated by any previous nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's people also suffered polytheism and disbelief, but Islahi says their extreme sexual corruption had to be addressed first, with other matters left for a later phase.
rows.anchor: However, people whose nature has been perverted to the extent that men seek men for sexual pleasure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi takes the discussion as evidence of the Qur’an's severe condemnation of sodomy.
rows.anchor: It can be estimated from this discussion the heinous status sodomy occupies in the eyes of the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls this the third aspect of Lot's censure and says the sentence's emphasis conveys its intensity.
rows.anchor: This is the third aspect of hate. Its intensity is apparent from the stress found in the sentence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijāl here means mature men.
rows.anchor: The word رﺟﺎل is also meaningful here because it is used for men of mature age.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording portrays a society in which licentiousness spreads across ages, erases sensitivity to age, and makes the perversion habitual.
rows.anchor: The consequence of this is that the sensitivity regarding age is done away with.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving women signifies wasted procreative energy; Islahi likens the choice to watering barren land while leaving crops dry, ending in civilizational ruin and humiliation in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The words “leaving aside women” depict the transformation that is the natural consequence of this perversion: creative energy is wasted in the pursuit of a totally wrong target.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them senseless and transgressing limits depicts rebellion against human nature and its consequences.
rows.anchor: The words “you are absolutely senseless; in fact, people who have crossed limits” depict their rebelliousness against human nature and its fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every sentence Lot spoke was meant to jolt his audience, but perverted, senseless people could not respond; their reply shows a society at its lowest point, where evil becomes everyone's habit and a fashion.
rows.anchor: It is evident from the style of the discourse that every sentence uttered by Lot (sws) was an eye-opener that was meant to jolt and shake them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Lot and his companions merely pose as pious shows that the people found his piety burdensome and wanted him to become like them.
rows.anchor: instead of regarding his piety to be a likeable trait, it weighed down heavily on them and they wanted him to become one of them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusation that Lot's group were pious implies some believed, but the rescue verse lists only his family, so Islahi infers that only family members believed.
rows.anchor: Had there been others besides them, they would have been mentioned among those who had been delivered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers were a small group, all within Lot's family: the threat calls them al-nās (“people”), while the rescue refers to them as ahl (“family”).
rows.anchor: small group professed faith in him as is evident from the word “people”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's wife was excluded because of her perversion, which may have been reinforced by her birth into that corrupt society.
rows.anchor: From among his family too, his wife was not included. Its obvious reason was her perversion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bias toward one's family and nation can obstruct truth; only attachment to God strong enough to overcome other feelings breaks that barrier.
rows.anchor: One’s bias towards one’s family and nation often becomes a hindrance in the cause of the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salvation requires seeking truth and sacrificing obstructive desires; marriage or kinship to a prophet cannot secure it, as shown by Lot's wife, Noah's son, Abraham's father, and Muhammad's uncle.
rows.anchor: even being the wife of a prophet or his son or father or uncle cannot earn him salvation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain sent on Lot's people was a rain of pebbles and stones.
rows.anchor: Here rain refers to the rain of pebbles and stones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A desert wind carried pebbles and stones onto caravans and settlements; Arabs call a storm that rains down pebbles ḥāṣib.
rows.anchor: The Arabs call it ﺣﺎﺻﺐ or a storm that rains down pebbles.

rows.speaker: Ust ādh Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī describes a dust storm that became a stone-hurling wind, first showering stones and then intensifying until it razed houses and covered them; he cites 29:40, 15:74, and 53:53–54.
rows.anchor: Ust ādh Farāhī, while referring to the details of this storm, writes: The Almighty unleashed a dust-laden storm on the people

rows.speaker: Ust ādh Farāhī
rows.claim: Islahi reports Farāhī's criticism that a translation error led Torah translators to misstate the whole incident; the excerpt begins the critique's summary but cuts off before its details.
